title: How Saudi Arabia Overextended Itself
author: Djene Rhys Bajalan
content:
![How Saudi Arabia Overextended
Itself](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/Mohammad_bin_Salman_in_Washington_-_2018_-40913857282-.jpg)

There are few projects that better capture Mohammed bin Salman's ambitions for
Saudi Arabia than NEOM. Announced in 2017 and launched as part of Vision 2030,
the vast development on the Red Sea was supposed to demonstrate what the
kingdom could accomplish when combining its almost limitless capital with
cutting-edge technology and political will. In its promotional materials, the
centerpiece of the project, The Line, was presented as an entirely new kind of
city stretching 170 kilometers through the desert. Saudi Arabia's Public
Investment Fund described NEOM as a "living laboratory" in which "innovation
will chart the course for a new future." Speaking in 2022, MBS declared the
project nothing short of a "civilizational revolution" that would "challenge
the traditional flat, horizontal cities" and "shine a light on alternative
ways to live."

But in recent years, skyrocketing costs, changing economic and political
circumstances, and the monumental engineering, infrastructure, and logistical
demands of the project have forced the Saudi government to scale back its
ambitions. By 2024, construction plans were reportedly concentrated on an
initial 2.4-kilometer section of the proposed 170-kilometer city. By October
2026, the Public Investment Fund acknowledged that The Line was no longer a
priority for completion by 2030, and plans for a spectacular elevated World
Cup stadium were reportedly shelved. It seems unlikely that whatever emerges
from the deserts of Tabuk Province will be anything like what the marketing
videos and slide decks once promised.

NEOM, in both its conception and its fate, is a Babelian monument to the
belief that sufficient wealth and political will could overcome the
constraints of geography, labor, and technology. As such, the scheme is
emblematic of a deeper contradiction within MBS's political project. Rising to
power in the mid-2010s, Saudi Arabia's _de facto_ ruler sought to use the
accumulated rents of the old oil economy to construct a new social order--a
technocratic, hypermodern, consumption-oriented society capable of projecting
economic and political power far beyond the Arabian Peninsula. This enterprise
brought significant changes to everyday life, including curbs on the religious
police, greater freedom for women to drive and travel independently, the
reopening of cinemas, and the expansion of public entertainment.
